lab_title: Human Heart Anatomy and Blood Flow
top_level_objectives: Identify the four chambers, four valves, and major vessels of the human heart.
Trace the pathway of blood through the heart and distinguish pulmonary from systemic circulation.
Explain how valve function prevents backflow and how ventricular wall thickness relates to pumping demand.

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the heart as a muscular pump and help students orient to its major visible surfaces and vessels before moving inside.
key_visuals: A large anatomical heart model centered in view with clear right/left orientation markers
Major vessels emerging from the superior aspect of the heart
Color contrast between deoxygenated and oxygenated sides
student_actions: Rotate the heart to identify anterior, posterior, superior, and inferior views.
Locate the major vessels and decide which side of the heart they connect to.
Use labels to distinguish right from left anatomy correctly.

scenes.brief_purpose: Focus on the internal chambers and establish how the heart is divided into right and left pumping sides.
key_visuals: A cutaway or opened heart showing the atria above and ventricles below
Distinct coloring or highlighting of the right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium, and left ventricle
The thicker left ventricular wall visible beside the thinner right ventricle
student_actions: Tap each chamber to name it and confirm its position.
Compare the thickness of the ventricular walls and note the difference.
Identify which chambers receive blood versus which chambers pump blood out.

scenes.brief_purpose: Show how the heart’s valves sit between chambers and vessels and how they enforce one-way flow.
key_visuals: Open views of the tricuspid, pulmonary, mitral, and aortic valves
Simple opening-and-closing motion to suggest the cardiac cycle
Arrows showing permitted flow direction and blocked backflow
student_actions: Match each valve to its correct location in the heart.
Observe how valve movement changes with pressure and flow direction.
Explain which valve blood passes through next at each step of the pathway.

scenes.brief_purpose: Trace deoxygenated blood returning from the systemic circulation into the right side of the heart.
key_visuals: Flow arrows entering from the superior and inferior vena cava into the right atrium
Highlighted pathway from right atrium through the tricuspid valve to the right ventricle
A clear separation between the returning body blood and the rest of the heart
student_actions: Follow the incoming blood pathway from the body to the right atrium.
Select the next structure in the sequence as blood moves to the right ventricle.
State why this blood is described as deoxygenated.

scenes.scene_name: To the Lungs and Back to the Left Heart
scenes.brief_purpose: Demonstrate pulmonary circulation and the return of oxygenated blood to the left side of the heart.
key_visuals: Pathway from the right ventricle through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary arteries
A simple lung visual or destination marker representing gas exchange
Pulmonary veins entering the left atrium with a distinct oxygenated color
student_actions: Trace blood from the right ventricle to the lungs and then back to the left atrium.
Identify the pulmonary valve, pulmonary arteries, and pulmonary veins in order.
Describe how this circuit differs from the systemic route.

scenes.scene_name: Left Heart to Systemic Outflow and Summary
scenes.brief_purpose: Complete the full circulation loop by showing blood leaving the left ventricle through the aorta and summarize the functional logic of the entire system.
key_visuals: Highlighted left ventricle pumping into the aortic valve and aorta
A strong visual emphasis on the thicker left ventricular myocardium
A complete loop diagram linking body, heart, lungs, and back to the body
student_actions: Trace the final steps of blood leaving the left ventricle into the aorta.
Explain why the left ventricle must generate more force than the right ventricle.
Review the full sequence of flow from body to heart to lungs and back to body.
